segments.t: Elise Formain arrives at the ASK agency following her departure from StarMedia. She gathers the team to deliver an ambitious welcome speech, hoping to smooth over past rivalries with Andrea Martel. However, an outraged Gabriel Sarda refuses to play along with the corporate welcome. Let's listen to their tense encounter in French first.
Merci à tous pour votre accueil chez ASK.
Bienvenue parmi nous dans notre équipe.
J'ai une réputation un peu difficile.
Ici, nous respectons le bon travail.
Je veux travailler avec vous deux.
Vous êtes de très bons agents.
Moi, je n'ai pas le temps.
Gabriel, reste un instant avec nous.
Je préfère retourner à mon bureau.
Nous pouvons quand même trinquer ensemble.
Je porte un toast très clair.
À la fin de nos principes!
Ton accueil est vraiment très direct!
Pardon, nous sommes tous très fatigués.
Let's examine the conversation line by line and explore the French expressions.
Merci à tous pour votre accueil chez ASK.
'Thank you all for your welcome at ASK.' Elise opens her speech with polite gratitude. The key noun here means 'welcome', anchored by its matching French article.
Bienvenue parmi nous dans notre équipe.
'Welcome among us to our team.' Andrea greets the newcomer warmly on behalf of the agency. The key noun here means 'welcome', anchored by its matching French article.
J'ai une réputation un peu difficile.
'I have a somewhat difficult reputation.' Elise frankly acknowledges her ruthless past at StarMedia. The verb meaning 'have' pairs naturally with the noun for 'reputation' in everyday conversation.
Ici, nous respectons le bon travail.
'Here, we respect good work.' Andrea emphasizes ASK's professional values. Notice how 'respect' leads directly into the noun meaning 'work'.
Je veux travailler avec vous deux.
'I want to work with you two.' Elise expresses her desire to collaborate with Andrea and Gabriel. Elise uses the polite 'you' form alongside 'want' to keep a respectful professional tone.
Vous êtes de très bons agents.
'You are very good agents.' Elise flatters the senior partners of ASK. The key noun here means 'agents', anchored by its matching French article.
Moi, je n'ai pas le temps.
'As for me, I do not have time.' Gabriel coldly rejects her attempts at charm. The verb meaning 'have' pairs naturally with the noun for 'time' in everyday conversation.
Gabriel, reste un instant avec nous.
'Gabriel, stay a moment with us.' Notice how 'stay' leads directly into the noun meaning 'moment'. Notice how 'stay' leads directly into the noun meaning 'moment'.
Je préfère retourner à mon bureau.
'I prefer to return to my office.' Gabriel makes an excuse to leave the reception. The verb meaning 'prefer' pairs naturally with the noun for 'office' in everyday conversation.
Nous pouvons quand même trinquer ensemble.
'We can still drink a toast together.' Elise attempts to maintain a convivial atmosphere. The clause hinges on the everyday verb meaning 'can'.
Je porte un toast très clair.
'I propose a very clear toast.' Gabriel steps forward with bitter sarcasm. The descriptive adjective for 'clear' agrees in gender and number with its noun.
À la fin de nos principes!
'To the end of our principles!' Gabriel raises his glass in solemn protest against the buyout. The key noun here means 'end', anchored by its matching French article.
Ton accueil est vraiment très direct!
'Your welcome is really very direct!' Elise reacts with cool poise to Gabriel's blunt hostility. Elise uses the casual singular 'you' with 'welcome', showing close familiarity.
Pardon, nous sommes tous très fatigués.

'Excuse us, we are all very tired.' Andrea apologizes to cover for her partner's explosive outburst. The key noun here means 'excuse us', anchored by its matching French article. Now let's listen to the complete discussion once more to reinforce the vocabulary.
